power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication

author.affiliation:
School of Optometry and Vision Science
								Faculty of Life Science
								Bar-Ilan University
								
									Israel

text.text: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices -a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied -as a remedy for the replication crisis.
text.formatted: Simmons, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011)</ref> proposed disclosure-based practices -a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied -as a remedy for the replication crisis.

text.text: Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward.
It did not.

Nine submissions over 2.5 years were unsuccessful (eight rejections and one withdrawal), largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework.

Here, I reflect on this experience, raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them, and offer recommendations for future practices.
To be honest, I am utterly confused.

How is it that we faced 9 failures to publish a successful replication explicitly following the disclosure practices proposed by Simmons et al., 2011 when the field of experimental psychology promotes replication studies as part of its "recovery plan" to overcome the replication crisis ?
text.formatted: How is it that we faced 9 failures to publish a successful replication explicitly following the disclosure practices proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Simmons et al., 2011</ref> when the field of experimental psychology promotes replication studies as part of its "recovery plan" to overcome the replication crisis ?

text.text: In 2022, my lab set out to test whether an effect we had published in PNAS (Masarwa et al., 2022) that larger images are better remembered during naturalistic encoding -would hold up online: different screens, different environments, no experimenter in the room, a more demographically varied sample than our lab studies ever reached.
text.formatted: In 2022, my lab set out to test whether an effect we had published in PNAS <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Masarwa et al., 2022)</ref> that larger images are better remembered during naturalistic encoding -would hold up online: different screens, different environments, no experimenter in the room, a more demographically varied sample than our lab studies ever reached.

text.text: Our paradigm involved long stretches of passive viewing with no responses required, which made it hard to know whether online participants were even watching the screen.
We built a method to confirm they were, and to exclude those who weren't.

After obtaining the data, we wrote the paper describing our replication and generalization online study and followed recommendations outlining procedures to overcome biases that are associated with the replication crisis (as sharing all the data and testing the effects before and after exclusion (Ioannidis, 2005; Simmons et al., 2011), see Figure 1).
text.formatted: After obtaining the data, we wrote the paper describing our replication and generalization online study and followed recommendations outlining procedures to overcome biases that are associated with the replication crisis (as sharing all the data and testing the effects before and after exclusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ioannidis, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Simmons et al., 2011)</ref>, see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The effect replicated robustly, even in our less optimal design.
I assumed, naively, that doing things this way would make publication straightforward.
It did not.
Our journey started in March 2023 and ended more than 2.5 years later, in Dec 2025.
We submitted our paper to 10 journals, 8 of which rejected our manuscript, and one that we withdrew from due to an excessive delay in editorial handling.

From 4 journals we got editorial rejections without reviews, and 4 journals rejected our manuscript after review, where one of these even allowed us to revise but after receiving our extensive revision the journal decided the revision was not sufficient.

The main take-home message I drew from this process and these reviews, alongside very valuable feedback, was that replicating lab results in online settings does not carry publication merit, unless accompanied by some theoretical novelty (Figure 2).
text.formatted: The main take-home message I drew from this process and these reviews, alongside very valuable feedback, was that replicating lab results in online settings does not carry publication merit, unless accompanied by some theoretical novelty (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: I then came to realize that this was why our manuscript had been rejected from one journal after another.
This was further echoed by several established cognitive experimental psychology colleagues of mine who shared these views.

In their view, a study that does not provide theoretical novelty on its own would not be publication-worthy to the field, even if it were a replication following the recommended field practices (e.g., Simmons et al., 2011).
text.formatted: In their view, a study that does not provide theoretical novelty on its own would not be publication-worthy to the field, even if it were a replication following the recommended field practices (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Simmons et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: At that point of our journey we reached a very positive turning point (and believe me, some of my grad students already thought it'd be best to just leave the paper as a preprint and abandon our goal to publish it in a peer-reviewed journal).
We were very fortunate to submit to Visual Cognition.

While here too we were informed that our manuscript lacked the theoretical depth to be a stand-alone manuscript, the editor and reviewers, instead of throwing us out the door (again), requested additional analyses that addressed a broader concern in the field -that accuracy in old-new recognition memory tasks may be biased, and that signal detection theory measures were needed to substantiate the effects we reported, as we indeed found.

Thus, while choosing to minimize the replication aspects of our paper, we followed all the practices proposed in the reviews, also adopting a wonderful method we now often use (Weidemann & Kahana, 2016) that allowed us to further substantiate our signal detection theory results.
text.formatted: Thus, while choosing to minimize the replication aspects of our paper, we followed all the practices proposed in the reviews, also adopting a wonderful method we now often use <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Weidemann & Kahana, 2016</ref>) that allowed us to further substantiate our signal detection theory results.

text.text: Our paper (Kreichman et al., 2025) was accepted after many additional analyses that improved it were performed.
text.formatted: Our paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Kreichman et al., 2025)</ref> was accepted after many additional analyses that improved it were performed.

text.text: I am grateful that we were fortunate to receive this constructive feedback and that our paper is finally out.
However, while our replication and generalization study has finally found a home, my confusion about whether the field is genuinely addressing the replication crisis remains.

This is especially puzzling when clear and straightforward recommendations (Ioannidis, 2005; Simmons et al., 2011) are available and the field promotes on a declarative level that it welcomes replications.
text.formatted: This is especially puzzling when clear and straightforward recommendations <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ioannidis, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Simmons et al., 2011)</ref> are available and the field promotes on a declarative level that it welcomes replications.

text.text: A replication to my understanding is repeating the same (or somewhat similar) methods and paradigm and observing an effect reported earlier.
In the same manner, failing to observe the effect under these experimental conditions constitutes a failure to replicate.

While theoretical novelty is clearly important in any scientific field, placing it as a prerequisite for publishing a replication significantly limits the replication testing arena and to my understanding prevents the field from testing reproducibility of many earlier findings.

Thus, there seems to be an existing ambiguity in the field about publishing replications that is to some degree unresolved (perhaps representing a gap between intentions or declarations vs practice and reality).

The situation we are currently in raises several critical questions that the field may want to reconsider: • Does the field wholeheartedly support replications if they are not accompanied by theoretical or practical novelty?
• Are transparent replications following recommended practices on their own not a substantiation of science and perhaps the most robust evidence for existing effects?
• When is a replication study desirable?
• How can a researcher that did not preregister their study know if the replication is publicationworthy or not?
In other words: shall a researcher aim to replicate earlier findings or not?
While the field has made substantial progress towards overcoming the replication crisis, for example by adopting open science practices such as sharing data and study preregistration, hurdles remain.

The field should be attentive to the critical questions raised above, as conducting replications and reporting their outcomes are among the most direct tests of whether an effect is real, even in the absence of theoretical novelty.

Therefore, I suggest that, in addition to the practices the field has already adopted, the field should pave the way for the publication of stand-alone replications of earlier findings that follow the practices presented in Simmons et al. (2011).
text.formatted: Therefore, I suggest that, in addition to the practices the field has already adopted, the field should pave the way for the publication of stand-alone replications of earlier findings that follow the practices presented in <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Simmons et al. (2011)</ref>.

text.text: Several routes could achieve this: (i) editorial policies stating explicitly that theoretical novelty is not required for replications; (ii) dedicated article types for replications, with criteria applied to methodological rigor and transparency rather than novelty; (iii) review procedures that evaluate a replication on its design and reporting before its outcome is known, as in results-blind review; and (iv) predetermined criteria for deciding which findings are "replication-worthy", such as findings that are influential or controversial, supported by few studies, or substantiated only in specific populations and settings.
Such replications, whether they confirm or fail to confirm an effect, may lack theoretical novelty, yet their publication is an essential step in scientific knowledge building and progress.
Without these changes, the field risks extensive loss of knowledge and valuable resources, counter to transparency in science.
